sources.text:
A scheduler chooses which ready job receives the processor. Turnaround time equals completion time minus arrival time. Response time equals the first time a job runs minus its arrival time. These metrics measure different things: early access to a processor does not necessarily imply early completion. First-come, first-served runs jobs in arrival order without preempting them. Shortest Job First selects the shortest available job and is non-preemptive. Shortest Time-to-Completion First is preemptive and selects the job with the least remaining processing time. Comparisons involving these shortest-job policies must state how execution lengths are known.

Round Robin rotates through a ready queue, running each selected job for at most one time slice before moving an unfinished job to the back. Shorter slices can improve initial responsiveness but increase the frequency of context switches. Larger slices amortize switching costs but can lengthen waits before a different job first runs. Neither a smaller average response time nor a smaller switching fraction alone establishes that a policy is best for every objective.

A multi-level feedback queue, or MLFQ, uses observed execution behavior instead of requiring exact future job lengths. Jobs in higher-priority queues run before lower-priority jobs; equal-priority jobs can share service by Round Robin. New jobs begin at high priority, and consuming the allowed CPU allotment causes demotion. Accounting for total consumed allotment prevents a job from retaining high priority indefinitely merely by yielding just before each slice ends. Periodic priority boosts can help jobs otherwise left waiting at low priority. Queue levels, slice lengths, allotments, and boost intervals are policy parameters, not universal constants.

This fixture adds an explicit scheduling model for exercises. It is authored example scaffolding rather than text copied from a textbook. Unless a question states otherwise, there is one processor, jobs are independent, and each job consists of one CPU burst with no I/O. Arrival times and required CPU service are provided. The processor never serves two jobs simultaneously. Time spent switching is not CPU service delivered to any job. A job that finishes before its slice ends does not use the remaining slice. If a job arrives at exactly a slice boundary, the question must say whether that arrival is enqueued before or after the preempted job. Ties must be resolved by an explicit rule, such as alphabetical job names.

A question that includes switching overhead must define when that overhead applies: for example, only when moving between different jobs, with no initial dispatch charge. It must also state whether arrivals can occur while switching and how they enter the queue. Questions that ignore overhead must say so. These conventions make a timeline reproducible and prevent a numeric answer from depending on unstated simulator behavior.

A comparison can report each job's first-run and completion times, then compute the requested averages. A design recommendation also needs an objective and constraints, such as a maximum response time, a switching budget, or a fairness requirement. A policy can satisfy one constraint while losing on another metric. Choosing a scheduler should therefore follow the stated workload and requirements. Hypothetical burst lengths and budgets introduced in an exercise are not measured workload traces, and labels assigned by the generator are not empirical student difficulty measurements.

questions.focus: Choosing among given Round Robin time-slice configurations under switch overhead using mean response and switch-count tradeoffs
questions.learning_goal: Integrate the definitions of response time, turnaround time and context-switch cost to judge a small set of fully specified Round Robin slice choices, deciding which configuration satisfies a stated mean-response requirement without exceeding a stated switching budget, and explaining why a single metric cannot settle the choice.
requirements: The question must supply one finite single-processor workload of independent jobs, each with an arrival time and one CPU burst, along with at most four named Round Robin time-slice configurations to compare.

It must state the overhead convention explicitly: when switching cost applies, that no switching charge is applied initially, whether arrivals can occur during switching, and how such arrivals enter the ready queue; configurations that ignore overhead must be labelled as doing so.
It must fix tie-breaking, the treatment of a job finishing before its slice ends, and whether an arrival at an exact slice boundary is enqueued before or after the preempted job.

The task must require reporting mean response time and switch count (and mean turnaround time where relevant) for each configuration, then selecting the configurations satisfying a stated maximum mean response together with a stated switching budget, and justifying the selection when the constraints conflict.
The answer must explain why smaller slices improving initial responsiveness does not by itself show a policy is best, and no configuration may be selected on a metric outside the stated objective.

questions.focus: Evaluating given MLFQ parameter sets that account for total consumed allotment and use periodic priority boosts
questions.learning_goal: Analyze how a multi-level feedback queue's demotion rule based on cumulative consumed allotment and its boost interval affect jobs that repeatedly yield before using a full slice, and evaluate which supplied parameter set meets a stated fairness or maximum-waiting constraint for a given workload.
requirements: The question must describe a concrete MLFQ setup with explicit queue levels, slice lengths, per-level allotments, a demotion rule, and a periodic priority-boost interval, offered as two or three named parameter sets rather than an open-ended design task.

It must state that demotion accounts for total consumed CPU allotment so that a job cannot keep high priority merely by yielding just before each slice ends, and require the answer to trace the priority path of at least one such yielding job under each supplied parameter set.

It must fix the workload, arrival times, service lengths, round-robin behaviour among equal-priority jobs, tie-breaking, and the treatment of switching overhead (including explicitly stating when overhead is ignored).

The task must require judging which parameter set satisfies a stated objective and constraint, such as a maximum waiting time for a low-priority job or a fairness requirement, while noting the cost the choice imposes on another stated metric.

The answer must treat queue levels, slice lengths, allotments and boost intervals as policy parameters rather than universal constants, and must not rely on prior knowledge of a particular operating system's scheduler.
